job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Sam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live at home above my dad's garage in Pellham, and I start the day by helping in the workshop till nine. Dad's an auto electrician and I like working beside him, mostly because it keeps my hands busy. After that I do applications at the kitchen table. I finished electrical engineering eight months ago, top of my class, and my final project was a backup power controller for a village clinic. I did internships at a regional power company and a switchgear maker. On Sundays I help at church with the sound system, and some of the older men there keep asking when I'll start a proper job. I ask myself the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because it means we aren't throwing away good work for a fashion. I'd tell the men at church that skilled trades and real engineering still count. I don't use social media. I'd just say it over a cup of tea after the service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the world stays roughly as it is, which isn't bad but isn't an answer for me either. I've sent 60 applications and had four interviews, and no offer. I'm on my parents' roof, which I'm grateful for and a bit ashamed of. I have about six weeks of savings and a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, and I'd take some hours at Dad's garage officially, with a small wage, to build my share. I'd ask the power company's apprenticeship manager again, since I know him. And I'd go to the local trade association's job fair, in a suit, with copies of my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy. I feel I should have a job by now, and I don't like feeling that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're ashamed. What is that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's how I was raised. A man should pay his way by twenty-three. Dad started at sixteen. I know the market is different, but the old voice doesn't care about the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the slow market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Large firms that let go of their apprentice schemes to save money, and a government that taxes small firms heavily so they can't hire. A small garage like Dad's would take a trainee tomorrow if the paperwork wasn't such a burden.

say: I'd say it's good we aren't throwing away **good work** for a fashion.
I'd tell the men at church that **skilled trades** and real engineering still count.
think: The world stays as it is, which is not bad but is **no answer** for me.
I'm grateful to my parents but a little **ashamed** to still live at home.
do: Work **paid hours** at Dad's garage to build my share.
Ask the power company's **apprenticeship manager** again.
Go to the trade association's **job fair** in a suit with copies of my CV.
feel: A bit **heavy**, because I feel I should have a job by now.
S0.quote: A small garage like Dad's would take a trainee tomorrow if the paperwork wasn't such a burden.
fieldNote: Sam links **shame** to how he was raised: a man pays his way by twenty-three.
He blames **big firms** dropping apprentice schemes and tax burdens on small firms.
Does not use AI or social media; he **speaks face to face**.

steps.text: Work paid hours at Dad's garage while applying
Ask the power company's apprenticeship manager about a place
Go to the trade association's job fair with printed CVs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this sounds like a salesman's promise. Some of it will be real, mostly in offices, and I'd tell friends to keep a skill with their hands. I'd also say firms shouldn't be allowed to drop people without a plan for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking jobs get taken, then design work and drawing offices shrink, and that's the entry door for people like me. Switchgear and power work still need hands. I haven't used the tools, and I don't plan to start, because I don't trust what they make up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on the physical side: installation, testing and maintenance of power equipment. I'd ask Dad if his garage could add electric vehicle charger installs, since that's work he's started getting asked about. I'd also ask the church community whether anyone knows a firm that's hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd put my head down and keep walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the tools. What if firms ask for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn the bare minimum, like using a calculator, and no more. I won't trust one to make a decision about a live circuit. If someone wants me to, they can sign the paper, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask the government for anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not handouts. I'd ask for support for apprenticeships, with simple paperwork and small firms rewarded for taking trainees. People should work for what they get, but they need a door to walk through.

I'd tell friends to keep a skill with their **hands**.
think: Drawing offices shrink, and that's the **entry door** for people like me.

Ask Dad about adding **EV charger** installs to the garage.
Ask people at **church** who knows a firm that's hiring.
feel: **Uneasy**; I'd put my head down and keep walking.
S1.quote: People should work for what they get, but they need a door to walk through.
fieldNote: Sam draws a line at **accountability**: whoever signs the paper owns the decision.
He wants **apprenticeship support**, not handouts: a door to walk through.
He turns the family garage into a real **business idea**: EV charger installs.

steps.text: Apply for installation, testing and maintenance roles at power firms
Ask the church community for a lead on firms that are hiring
Add EV charger installs to Dad's garage services
Hold off on any AI tool until a firm requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a flood, and I'd say that out loud. I'd tell people at church to look after one another, and to put money aside. I'd say governments should slow things until families and firms can keep up, even if that costs growth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My degree is worth far less if thinking work is done by machines, and I haven't started yet. The robots for hands-on work come about 2031, so I'd have three years in the physical trades. I'd be starting as a young man with a gap of a few years in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the physical side right away: I'd join Dad's garage full time and train as an electrician with a recognised licence. I'd cut spending to the bone and give up my phone plan. I'd also ask the church's helping fund about a short loan, if I needed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Afraid, mostly. I'd keep it to myself, which is bad, but that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep it to yourself. Who would you talk to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my pastor and my dad, in that order. Dad would say fix a car, solve the next problem. The pastor would ask me to pray, and I'd do that too. I'd still rather have a plan alongside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your plan be for a family of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put off asking my girlfriend Hannah to marry me. I'd want a steady job first. She'd say wait, I don't mind, and I'd feel the guilt of her waiting on my account.

say: I'd say it's a **flood**, and governments should slow things until families keep up.
I'd tell the church to **look after one another** and put money aside.
think: My degree is worth far less if machines do the thinking, and I haven't **started** yet.
Robots hold off until about 2031, so I'd have **three years** in the physical trades.
do: Join Dad's **garage** full time and train for an electrician's licence.
Cut spending to the bone and give up my **phone plan**.
Ask the church's **helping fund** about a short loan if needed.
feel: **Afraid**, mostly, and I'd keep it to myself.
S2.quote: Dad would say fix a car, solve the next problem. The pastor would ask me to pray, and I'd do that too.
fieldNote: Sam keeps fear **private** and relies on his pastor and his father.

He shifts to a **licensed trade** in the family garage.

steps.text: Join Dad's garage full time and train for an electrician's licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a stretch of road you can see the end of. I'd say people should plan, not panic. I'd tell the men at church that their sons should learn a trade and a bit of business too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough to put a good foundation under me. I'd be a licensed electrician with a few years' experience before robots can do my work, around 2034. That gives me time to own a share of a business, which is more secure than a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job offered, apprenticeship or engineering, and work hard. I'd study for my electrician's licence at night. I'd save a third of every pay and try to put down a deposit on a small unit near the garage. And I'd ask Dad to think about making the garage a partnership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. Not happy, but steady, like standing on a firm floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does owning a share of a business matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wage can be cut by someone you've never met, but a share you hold yourself, you can defend. My granddad had a small shop for forty years, and it fed the whole family through bad times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you want to be remembered in that five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As someone who kept his word and kept the lights on, literally. I'd like to say I helped my dad's business grow and that I brought a few young lads through an apprenticeship.

say: I'd say people should **plan, not panic**, and sons should learn a trade and some business.
I'd tell church friends a **foundation** matters more than a fashion.
think: Five years is enough to be a **licensed electrician** before robots can do my work, around 2034.
Owning a **share** of a business is safer than a wage.
do: Take the first **job or apprenticeship** and study for my electrician's licence at night.
Save a **third** of every pay for a deposit near the garage.
Ask Dad to make the garage a **partnership**.
feel: **Steady**, like standing on a firm floor, but not happy.
S3.quote: A wage can be cut by someone you've never met, but a share you hold yourself, you can defend.
fieldNote: Sam sees **ownership** as security: a wage can be cut by a stranger.
His granddad's **shop** gives him a family picture of resilience.
He wants to help bring young lads through an **apprenticeship**.

steps.text: Take the first job or apprenticeship offered and work hard

Save a third of every pay for a deposit near the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it to other graduates, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is time enough to do it properly. I'd say don't sit around, and don't leave everything to government either. I'd tell friends to build something that lasts, like a trade, a family or a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine. In ten years I'd be an experienced electrician with a stake in the garage. Even if robots arrive around 2039, the person who owns the work and the customers stays needed. I'd also have a family by then, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a job in the first year, finish my licence in two, and marry Hannah by twenty-six. I'd buy a small house in Pellham by thirty. I'd keep a savings pot for slow months and teach young apprentices on Saturdays through the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd be busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you even in that ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's health, honestly. He's 58 and his back is bad. If he couldn't work, the garage would depend on me earlier than we've planned. I'd want us to have a plan well before that day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you treat the AI tools in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, with care. I'd let others try them first, and use them if they've proven safe for my kind of work. I'm not against progress, I just want proof.

I'd tell friends to build something that **lasts**, like a trade or a family.
think: In ten years I'd be an **experienced electrician** with a stake in the garage.
Whoever owns the **work and customers** stays needed, even after robots arrive.

S4.quote: I'm not against progress, I just want proof.
fieldNote: Sam's calm rests on **family plans**: marriage, a house and a business stake.
His fear is for his **father's health** more than AI.

steps.text: Take an engineering or apprentice job within the first year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no room for a young man to get his feet under him. What would help is apprenticeships with simple paperwork, small firms rewarded for hiring trainees, and families and the church holding together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people take silence for confidence. I'm quiet because I was raised to be, not because I'm sure. I'd like someone to say, plainly, here's a door and here's what to do.

headlineQuote: People take silence for confidence. I'm quiet because I was raised to be, not because I'm sure.
portrait: Sam is a 23-year-old **electrical engineering** graduate, top of his class, living above his father's garage in Pellham.
He has made 60 applications, had four interviews and carries a loan with six weeks of **savings** and some shame.
He is traditional and free-market, wants **apprenticeships** and ownership over handouts, and leans on church and family.
He never uses AI tools, distrusts them for work such as **live circuits**, and moves toward the hands-on trades.
His plan is to become a licensed electrician, take a share in the **garage** and marry Hannah.
biggestWorry: The two-year **AGI** picture worries him most, since a young man would have no time to find his feet.
whatWouldHelp: He wants simple **apprenticeship** schemes, small firms rewarded for training and the support of church and family.
